stem: Why must an organization's digital accessibility evaluation strategy combine automated testing tools with human manual testing?

options.text: Because automated scanners are better suited to readability and plain language, while manual testers validate DOM syntax rules.
options.shortLabel: Scanners test readability; humans test syntax
options.rationale: This inverts reality: automated tools are suited to machine-checkable DOM syntax and rules, whereas human evaluators are needed for subjective qualities like plain language, cognitive flow, and context.

options.text: Because automated scanners detect only a subset of barriers and cannot evaluate contextual meaning, logical flow, or usability.
options.shortLabel: Scanners catch partial issues; humans assess context
options.rationale: Automated testing catches machine-testable issues such as missing attributes and insufficient color contrast, but human evaluation is essential to judge contextual meaning, keyboard navigation, and actual screen reader usability.

options.text: Because regulators accept manual audit reports as proof of conformance while automated scan results are treated as preliminary evidence.
options.shortLabel: Manual reports accepted as sole proof
options.rationale: No accessibility standard or regulation treats manual reports as the sole proof of conformance; conformance evaluation combines automated checks, manual review, and assistive technology testing.

options.text: Because automated evaluation engines cannot execute client-side JavaScript, leaving them unable to audit single-page web applications.
options.rationale: Modern automated tools (such as Axe-core and Lighthouse) run directly inside browser rendering engines and readily parse client-side JavaScript; their limitation is human judgment, not script execution.

explanation: A complete digital accessibility evaluation strategy requires both automated and manual testing. Automated testing tools provide speed and scale, catching syntax errors, missing attributes, and other machine-testable issues across thousands of pages. However, they can check only a limited subset of WCAG requirements and cannot determine whether alternative text is meaningful in context, whether keyboard focus follows a logical sequence, or whether complex dynamic widgets are truly usable with assistive technology like screen readers. Human manual testing bridges this critical gap.

references.title: W3C Web Accessibility Initiative: Evaluating Web Accessibility Overview
